title: Observability and Reliability
subtitle: Metrics, logs, SLOs, resilience and incident response
description: Build the monitoring pipeline, define SLOs with burn-rate alerts, make workloads survive disruption and run incidents with the right debugging tools.
outcomes: Wire metrics-server, Prometheus, ServiceMonitors and kube-state-metrics
Collect structured logs and traces with OpenTelemetry
Alert on error-budget burn instead of raw thresholds

modules.title: Observability
modules.summary: Metrics, logs, traces and alerting on SLOs.

lessons.title: The Kubernetes metrics pipeline
lessons.summary: metrics-server for kubectl top and HPA, Prometheus for history, ServiceMonitor for discovery and kube-state-metrics for object state.
objectives: Distinguish the resource metrics API from a full monitoring pipeline
Scrape an application with a ServiceMonitor
Explain what kube-state-metrics adds and write useful PromQL

sections.title: Two pipelines, two jobs
sections.body:
Kubernetes has **two separate metrics paths**. The **resource metrics pipeline** is served by `metrics-server`: it scrapes the kubelet on every node, keeps only the latest sample in memory and exposes it through the `metrics.k8s.io` API. It powers `kubectl top` and the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, and nothing else. It has no history and no custom metrics.

The **full monitoring pipeline** is usually Prometheus (often installed with the kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart). It scrapes the kubelet/cAdvisor, your applications, and `kube-state-metrics` (which turns the state of API objects into metrics), stores time series and lets you query, graph and alert on them. In production you run both: metrics-server for autoscaling, Prometheus for everything else.

sections.title: What each component provides
head: Component
Data source
Retention
Used for
rows: kubelet /metrics/resource (CPU, memory per pod and node)
Any /metrics endpoint: kubelet, cAdvisor, apps, exporters
Days to weeks on local disk (default 15d)
The Kubernetes API (Deployments, Pods, Nodes, Jobs...)
Replica counts, pod phase, restart counts, requests/limits
Node OS: disk, network, load, filesystem

sections.title: About this example: metrics-server in action
sections.body: The block below checks that the `metrics.k8s.io` API is registered and then reads live usage. Run it on any cluster where metrics-server is installed; the `AVAILABLE True` line proves the aggregated API works. In `kubectl top`, the CPU column is in millicores (`m`) and memory in mebibytes (`Mi`), averaged over the last scrape window, not a historic peak.

sections.title: Verify metrics-server and read usage
sections.code:
kubectl get apiservice v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io
kubectl top nodes
kubectl top pods -n shop --sort-by=memory
sections.output:
NAME                     SERVICE                      AVAILABLE   AGE
v1beta1.metrics.k8s.io   kube-system/metrics-server   True        41d

NAME       CPU(cores)   CPU%   MEMORY(bytes)   MEMORY%
node-a     412m         10%    3120Mi          41%
node-b     988m         24%    5410Mi          71%

NAME                       CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
checkout-7d9c6b8f5-x2k4p   240m         512Mi
checkout-7d9c6b8f5-q8wzr   231m         498Mi
web-5f7b9d8c6-m4t2n        12m          64Mi
sections.note: If AVAILABLE shows False (MissingEndpoints), `kubectl top` fails with 'Metrics API not available'. On clusters with self-signed kubelet certificates, metrics-server needs --kubelet-insecure-tls only in test environments.

sections.title: About this example: scraping an app with a ServiceMonitor
sections.body: With the Prometheus Operator you do not edit prometheus.yml. A **ServiceMonitor** selects Services by label and tells Prometheus which named port and path to scrape. Apply this file with `kubectl apply -f servicemonitor.yaml`; look at `selector.matchLabels` (must match the Service labels), `port` (the Service port name, not number) and `release: kube-prometheus-stack`, which is the label the Prometheus instance uses to pick up monitors in the default Helm install.

sections.title: ServiceMonitor for the checkout service
sections.code:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: ServiceMonitor
metadata:
  name: checkout
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    release: kube-prometheus-stack
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: checkout
  namespaceSelector:
    matchNames:
      - shop
  endpoints:
    - port: metrics
      path: /metrics
      interval: 30s
      scrapeTimeout: 10s
sections.note: Requires the monitoring.coreos.com CRDs. Verify with: kubectl get servicemonitor -n shop. Then open Prometheus > Status > Targets and look for serviceMonitor/shop/checkout/0 in state UP.

sections.title: Empty targets usually means a label mismatch
sections.body: If the target never appears, check three things in order: the ServiceMonitor carries the label your Prometheus `serviceMonitorSelector` expects, its `selector.matchLabels` matches the **Service** (not the Pod) labels, and the `port` is the Service's port **name**. A Service with an unnamed port cannot be scraped by a ServiceMonitor.

sections.title: About this example: PromQL against cAdvisor and kube-state-metrics
sections.body: These queries are what you type into the Prometheus expression browser (or Grafana). The first set uses cAdvisor series (`container_*`) from the kubelet, the second uses kube-state-metrics (`kube_*`). Each sample result is an instant vector: labels on the left, the current value on the right. Pay attention to `rate()` over counters and to `sum by` to collapse per-container series into per-pod or per-namespace totals.

sections.title: Useful PromQL with sample results
sections.code:
# CPU cores used per pod (5m rate of a counter)
sum by (pod) (rate(container_cpu_usage_seconds_total{namespace="shop",container!=""}[5m]))
{pod="checkout-7d9c6b8f5-x2k4p"}  0.241
{pod="checkout-7d9c6b8f5-q8wzr"}  0.233

# Working-set memory vs limit (ratio near 1 means OOM risk)
max by (pod) (container_memory_working_set_bytes{namespace="shop",container!=""})
  / max by (pod) (kube_pod_container_resource_limits{namespace="shop",resource="memory"})
{pod="checkout-7d9c6b8f5-x2k4p"}  0.94

# Pods not ready per namespace
sum by (namespace) (kube_pod_status_ready{condition="false"})
{namespace="shop"}  2

# Containers restarted in the last hour
sum by (pod) (increase(kube_pod_container_status_restarts_total[1h])) > 0
{pod="worker-6c4d-zq7lp"}  7

# Deployments with fewer available replicas than desired
kube_deployment_spec_replicas - kube_deployment_status_replicas_available > 0
{deployment="checkout",namespace="shop"}  1
sections.note: Use the working set (container_memory_working_set_bytes), not usage_bytes: it is what the kubelet compares against the limit when deciding to OOM-kill.

exercises.title: Read live resource usage
exercises.prompt: Confirm the Metrics API is available, then list the five heaviest pods by memory across all namespaces.
exercises.expected: A header line plus five pods, sorted by memory descending, with CPU in millicores and memory in Mi.
exercises.hint: Metrics need ~1 minute after pod creation to appear.

exercises.title: Find crash-looping pods with PromQL
exercises.prompt: In Prometheus, write a query returning pods that restarted more than 3 times in the last hour.
exercises.expected: One series per qualifying pod with its restart count as value; empty if none.
exercises.hint: Counters need increase() or rate(), never the raw value.

questions.question: Which component stores history and supports alerting?
questions.explain: metrics-server keeps only the latest sample; Prometheus stores time series and evaluates alert rules.

questions.question: A ServiceMonitor target does not appear. What should you check first?
options: Label selectors and the named Service port
questions.explain: ServiceMonitors select Services by label and reference the port name, and Prometheus must select the monitor itself.

questions.question: Why wrap container_cpu_usage_seconds_total in rate()?
options: It is a counter that only increases
questions.explain: Counters grow monotonically; rate() converts them to per-second usage, i.e. CPU cores.

questions.question: What does kube-state-metrics export?
options: Object state derived from the Kubernetes API
questions.explain: It watches the API server and exposes replica counts, pod phases, restarts, requests and limits as metrics.

lessons.title: Logging and tracing
lessons.summary: Log collection patterns, structured JSON logs and OpenTelemetry basics for following a request across services.
objectives: Compare node-agent, sidecar and direct-push log collection
Emit structured logs that can be queried by field
Explain traces, spans and the OpenTelemetry Collector

sections.title: Containers write to stdout, something else ships it
sections.body:
Kubernetes does not store logs long term. A container that writes to stdout/stderr has its output captured by the container runtime into a file on the node (`/var/log/pods/...`), which is what `kubectl logs` reads. When the pod is deleted or the node is rotated, those files go with it, and the kubelet rotates them by size (default 10Mi, 5 files).

So a logging architecture always needs a **collector** that moves logs off the node into a searchable store such as Loki, Elasticsearch or a cloud service. Metrics tell you *that* something is wrong; logs tell you *what happened*; traces tell you *where* in a chain of services the time went.

sections.title: Log collection patterns
head: Pattern
How it works
Pros
Cons
rows: Fluent Bit / Promtail / Vector tails /var/log/pods on each node
One per node, no app change, standard choice
Only sees stdout/stderr and mounted files
A second container tails a file the app writes into a shared emptyDir
Handles apps that only write files; per-app parsing
The app sends logs to the backend over the network
Couples app to backend; loses logs on outage
No history, lost with the pod

sections.title: About this example: a node log agent as a DaemonSet
sections.body: This manifest runs Fluent Bit on every node and mounts the host's `/var/log` read-only so it can tail container logs. Apply it with `kubectl apply -f fluent-bit.yaml`. Look at the `hostPath` volume, the `tolerations` (so it also runs on tainted nodes) and the resource limits that stop the agent starving workloads. The ConfigMap with the pipeline is omitted here for brevity, so the pod will start but needs your output configuration.

sections.title: Fluent Bit DaemonSet
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: fluent-bit
  namespace: default
  labels:
    app: fluent-bit
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: fluent-bit
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: fluent-bit
    spec:
      tolerations:
        - operator: Exists
      containers:
        - name: fluent-bit
          image: cr.fluentbit.io/fluent/fluent-bit:3.1
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi}
            limits: {memory: 128Mi}
          volumeMounts:
            - name: varlog
              mountPath: /var/log
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: varlog
          hostPath:
            path: /var/log
sections.note: Check rollout with: kubectl rollout status ds/fluent-bit. One pod per node should be Running.

sections.title: About this example: unstructured vs structured logs
sections.body: The block contrasts the same event written two ways. Free text needs a regex to extract fields and breaks when the message wording changes. A JSON line carries stable keys, so your log backend can filter by `level`, `status` or `trace_id` without parsing. The output of `kubectl logs` shows what the collector will ingest; the last command shows a LogQL query (Loki) filtering on those fields.

sections.title: Structured logging and querying
sections.code:
kubectl logs deploy/checkout -n shop --tail=2

# LogQL (Loki): errors for one trace
# {namespace="shop", app="checkout"} | json | level="error" | trace_id="4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736"
sections.note: Always log the trace_id: it is the join key between logs and traces. Never log secrets, tokens or full card numbers.

sections.title: About this example: OpenTelemetry Collector configuration
sections.body: A **trace** is the path of one request; each hop is a **span** with a start time, duration and parent. The OpenTelemetry Collector receives spans from applications (OTLP), batches them and exports to a backend such as Tempo or Jaeger. This file is a Collector config (not a Kubernetes object, so it uses language `text`) normally stored in a ConfigMap and mounted at `/etc/otelcol/config.yaml`. Read the three pipeline stages in order: `receivers`, `processors`, `exporters`, joined under `service.pipelines`.

sections.title: otel-collector config.yaml
sections.code:
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318
processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 400
  k8sattributes: {}
  batch:
    timeout: 5s
exporters:
  otlp/tempo:
    endpoint: tempo.observability.svc:4317
    tls:
      insecure: true
service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, k8sattributes, batch]
      exporters: [otlp/tempo]
sections.note: The k8sattributes processor adds pod, namespace and node labels to every span, so you can pivot from a slow trace to the pod that served it. Applications only need OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4317.

sections.title: The three signals compared
head: Signal
Question it answers
Cardinality cost
Typical store
rows: Is something wrong, and how much?
Where did the time go across services?

exercises.prompt: Fetch the previous instance's logs of a pod that restarted and the last 20 lines with timestamps.
exercises.expected: Time-prefixed lines from the container instance that crashed.
exercises.hint: Use -c NAME when a pod has several containers.

exercises.title: Follow many pods at once
exercises.prompt: Stream logs from all pods behind a label for the last 5 minutes.
exercises.hint: --max-log-requests raises the default limit of 5 concurrent streams.

questions.question: Where does kubectl logs read from?
options: The log file the runtime keeps on the node
questions.explain: The kubelet serves the file the container runtime writes under /var/log/pods on that node.

questions.question: Which pattern is the standard way to collect stdout logs from every node?
questions.explain: A DaemonSet runs one collector per node and tails the node's container log files.

questions.question: What links a log line to a distributed trace?
options: A trace_id field logged with the event
questions.explain: Putting the trace id in each log line lets you jump between the two signals.

questions.question: What does the OpenTelemetry Collector's batch processor do?
options: Groups telemetry before export to reduce requests
questions.explain: Batching reduces export overhead and smooths bursts.

lessons.title: Alerting, SLIs and SLOs
lessons.summary: Define service level indicators, set SLOs and error budgets, and alert on burn rate with a PrometheusRule.
objectives: Define an SLI, SLO and error budget with real numbers
Explain why burn-rate alerts beat static thresholds
Write a multi-window PrometheusRule and route it with Alertmanager

sections.title: Alert on user pain, not on causes
sections.body:
A **Service Level Indicator (SLI)** is a measurement of user-visible quality, usually a ratio: good events divided by valid events (for example, requests answered without a 5xx in under 300 ms). A **Service Level Objective (SLO)** is the target for that ratio over a window, such as 99.9% over 30 days. The **error budget** is what remains: 100% minus the SLO.

Alerting on CPU above 80% pages people for things users never notice. Alerting on **budget burn** pages people only when users are being hurt fast enough to threaten the objective. This is the approach of the Google SRE workbook and it works well with Prometheus.

sections.title: SLO targets and what they allow
head: SLO (30 days)
Error budget
Allowed downtime
Meaning
rows: Needs multi-region and automation; very costly

sections.title: About this example: recording the SLI
sections.body: These Prometheus recording rules turn raw request counters into an error ratio at several windows. They live inside a PrometheusRule object, applied with `kubectl apply -f`, and the operator loads them into Prometheus. Look at `rate(...[5m])` for the short window and `[1h]`, `[6h]` for long ones; the metric name `http_requests_total` and its `code` label are assumptions about your app. Recording the ratio once keeps the alert expressions cheap and readable.

sections.title: PrometheusRule: SLI recording rules
sections.code:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: checkout-sli
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    release: kube-prometheus-stack
spec:
  groups:
    - name: checkout.sli
      rules:
        - record: job:http_errors:ratio_rate5m
          expr: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",code=~"5.."}[5m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[5m]))
        - record: job:http_errors:ratio_rate1h
          expr: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout",code=~"5.."}[1h]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{job="checkout"}[1h]))
sections.note: Check that it loaded: kubectl get prometheusrule -n shop, then query job:http_errors:ratio_rate5m in Prometheus.

sections.title: Burn-rate alert tiers (SLO 99.9%, 30-day window)
head: Severity
Burn rate
Long window
Short window
Budget consumed

sections.title: About this example: multi-window burn-rate alerts
sections.body: Burn rate is the observed error ratio divided by the budget (0.001 for a 99.9% SLO). A rate of 14.4 sustained for an hour burns 2% of the monthly budget. Requiring both the long and the short window to exceed the threshold gives fast detection and fast reset: the short window stops the alert firing long after the problem is fixed. This second rule file is applied the same way; read the `expr` threshold `14.4 * 0.001`, the `for` duration and the `severity` label that Alertmanager routes on.

sections.title: PrometheusRule: burn-rate alerts
sections.code:
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PrometheusRule
metadata:
  name: checkout-slo-alerts
  namespace: shop
  labels:
    release: kube-prometheus-stack
spec:
  groups:
    - name: checkout.slo
      rules:
        - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetBurnFast
          expr: |
            job:http_errors:ratio_rate1h > (14.4 * 0.001)
            and
            job:http_errors:ratio_rate5m > (14.4 * 0.001)
          for: 2m
          labels:
            severity: page
          annotations:
            summary: Checkout is burning its 30d error budget 14x too fast
            description: Error ratio {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} over the last hour.
            runbook_url: https://runbooks.example.com/checkout-errors
        - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetBurnSlow
          expr: |
            job:http_errors:ratio_rate6h > (6 * 0.001)
            and
            job:http_errors:ratio_rate30m > (6 * 0.001)
          for: 15m
          labels:
            severity: ticket
          annotations:
            summary: Checkout error budget is burning steadily
sections.note: The slow alert needs ratio_rate6h and ratio_rate30m recording rules defined the same way as the 5m and 1h ones above.

sections.title: About this example: Alertmanager routing
sections.body: Alertmanager receives firing alerts, groups, deduplicates and sends them to receivers. This is an `alertmanager.yaml` fragment (language `text`, as it is not a Kubernetes object; with kube-prometheus-stack it is supplied through Helm values or an AlertmanagerConfig). The `route` tree sends `severity=page` to the on-call receiver and everything else to chat; `inhibit_rules` silence a lesser alert while a bigger one for the same service is firing.

sections.title: alertmanager.yaml route
sections.code:
route:
  receiver: slack-default
  group_by: [alertname, namespace]
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h
  routes:
    - matchers: [severity="page"]
      receiver: pagerduty-oncall
receivers:
  - name: slack-default
    slack_configs:
      - channel: '#alerts'
        api_url_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/slack-url
  - name: pagerduty-oncall
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/pd-key
inhibit_rules:
  - source_matchers: [severity="page"]
    target_matchers: [severity="ticket"]
    equal: [namespace]
sections.note: Keep webhook URLs and keys in Secrets mounted as files, never in the config text.

exercises.title: Compute the error budget
exercises.prompt: For a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, calculate the allowed downtime in minutes.
exercises.expected: 43.2 minutes of full outage per 30 days.

exercises.title: List loaded alert rules
exercises.prompt: Check which PrometheusRule objects exist and that Prometheus picked them up.
exercises.expected: A table of PrometheusRule objects with name and age; check Status > Rules in the Prometheus UI.
exercises.hint: Rules also need the label Prometheus selects on.

questions.question: What is an error budget?
questions.explain: It is the permitted amount of unreliability, e.g. 0.1% for a 99.9% SLO.

questions.question: Why combine a long and a short window in a burn-rate alert?
options: Fast detection plus quick reset after recovery
questions.explain: The long window shows significance; the short window ensures the problem is still happening.

questions.question: A burn rate of 1 means...
options: Budget is used exactly over the whole SLO window
Budget is gone in an hour
questions.explain: Burn rate 1 spends the budget exactly by the end of the window.

questions.question: Which is the best paging condition?
questions.explain: Page on user-visible symptoms that threaten the SLO.

modules.title: Reliability and incidents
modules.summary: Resilient workloads and calm incident response.

lessons.title: Resilience: probes, shutdown and disruption
lessons.summary: Probes done right, graceful shutdown, PodDisruptionBudgets, retries and timeouts, and small chaos experiments.
objectives: Choose liveness, readiness and startup probes that do not cause outages
Shut pods down gracefully with preStop and terminationGracePeriodSeconds
Protect availability with a PDB and validate with a chaos experiment

sections.title: Failure is normal; losing requests is not
sections.body:
Pods are deleted constantly: rollouts, node drains, autoscaling, spot reclaim. A resilient service handles each of those without dropping requests. Four mechanisms cooperate: **probes** decide when a pod receives traffic and when it is restarted, **graceful shutdown** lets in-flight requests finish, **PodDisruptionBudgets** limit voluntary disruption, and **client retries with timeouts** hide the rest.

The common failure is a probe that makes things worse: a liveness probe that checks the database restarts every pod when the database blips, turning a partial outage into a total one.

sections.title: Probes: use each for one purpose
head: Probe
Question
On failure
Good check
rows: Same endpoint as liveness, long budget (e.g. 30 x 10s)
Removed from Service endpoints; not restarted
Local dependencies it needs for requests
Is the process wedged for good?
Cheap in-process check; never external dependencies

sections.title: About this example: a Deployment with careful probes and shutdown
sections.body: This complete Deployment combines the settings of this lesson. Apply it with `kubectl apply -f web.yaml` and watch a rollout with `kubectl rollout status`. Look at three things: the `startupProbe` that gives slow boots up to 150 seconds, the `preStop` sleep that keeps the pod serving while endpoint removal propagates through kube-proxy and ingress, and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, which must be longer than preStop plus the app's own drain time.

sections.title: Deployment with probes and graceful shutdown
sections.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
  labels:
    app: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: nginx:1.27-alpine
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          startupProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 30
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 2
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /, port: 80}
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 10; nginx -s quit"]
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 50m, memory: 64Mi}
            limits: {memory: 128Mi}
sections.note: Shutdown timeline: pod marked Terminating, endpoints removed (in parallel), preStop runs 10s, then SIGTERM, then SIGKILL at 45s from the start.

sections.title: What happens when a pod is deleted

items.title: Terminating and endpoint removal
items.body: The API marks the pod Terminating. The endpoints controller removes it from Services, but kube-proxy, ingress and DNS caches learn about this with a delay, so traffic still arrives for a few seconds.

items.title: preStop hook
items.body: The kubelet runs preStop first. A short sleep keeps the app serving while the removal propagates.

items.title: SIGTERM
items.body: The container gets SIGTERM. The app must stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight work and exit. Make sure PID 1 receives the signal (use exec form, not a shell wrapper).

items.title: SIGKILL
items.body: After terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30, counted from step 1) the kubelet sends SIGKILL. Exit code 137 on a routine rollout means the grace period was too short.

sections.title: About this example: PodDisruptionBudget and observing it
sections.body: A **PDB** tells the eviction API how many pods of a set may be down during voluntary disruptions such as `kubectl drain` or cluster upgrades. This one keeps at least 2 of the 3 `web` pods available. Apply it, then try to drain; the `ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS` column shows how many evictions are currently permitted. PDBs do not guard against involuntary failures such as a node crash.

sections.title: PodDisruptionBudget for web
sections.code:
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: web-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
sections.note: After applying: kubectl get pdb  ->  NAME web-pdb, MIN AVAILABLE 2, MAX UNAVAILABLE N/A, ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS 1, AGE 8s. Never set minAvailable equal to replicas: the node can then never be drained.

sections.title: About this example: a chaos experiment
sections.body: Chaos engineering means breaking things on purpose in a controlled way to confirm your assumptions. This session kills one pod while a loop of requests measures the effect. Run the loop in one terminal and the delete in another; the hypothesis is that no request fails. Look at the `HTTP 200` counts and at how quickly the replacement pod becomes `Ready`. Tools such as Chaos Mesh and LitmusChaos automate network delay, pod kill and node faults on a schedule.

sections.title: Kill a pod while sending traffic
sections.code:
kubectl delete pod web-6d8f9c7b5-k2m8x --wait=false
kubectl get pods -l app=web -w
sections.output:
pod "web-6d8f9c7b5-k2m8x" deleted
NAME                   READY   STATUS        RESTARTS   AGE
web-6d8f9c7b5-k2m8x    1/1     Terminating   0          12m

lessons.title: Incident response and debugging
lessons.summary: Debug with ephemeral containers, recognise node, etcd and API server symptoms, and write a blameless postmortem.
objectives: Attach an ephemeral debug container with kubectl debug
Diagnose NotReady nodes and control-plane symptoms
Run an incident from mitigation to postmortem

sections.title: Mitigate first, understand later
sections.body:
During an incident the goal is to **restore service**, not to find root cause. A reliable order is: acknowledge and declare severity, assign roles (incident commander, communications, operators), mitigate (roll back, scale, fail over, disable a flag), verify recovery with the SLI, and only then investigate. Keep a timeline in a shared document as you go; it becomes the postmortem.

Kubernetes adds its own tooling for the investigation step. Minimal images have no shell or `curl`, so you cannot `kubectl exec` into them to look around. **Ephemeral containers** solve this by attaching a temporary debug container to the running pod.

sections.title: About this example: kubectl debug
sections.body: These commands add a throwaway `busybox` container to a running pod, sharing the target container's process namespace, so you can see its processes and network without restarting it. The second command copies a crashing pod with a different command so you can inspect it, and the third opens a shell on a node via a privileged pod with the host filesystem mounted at `/host`. Note the `Defaulting debug container name` line: that is the ephemeral container you are now inside.

sections.title: Ephemeral, copied and node debugging
sections.code:
kubectl debug -it checkout-7d9c6b8f5-x2k4p -n shop --image=busybox:1.36 --target=checkout
kubectl debug checkout-7d9c6b8f5-x2k4p -n shop --copy-to=checkout-debug --container=checkout -it -- sh
kubectl debug node/node-b -it --image=busybox:1.36
sections.output:
Targeting container "checkout". If you don't see processes from this container it may be because the container runtime doesn't support this feature.
Defaulting debug container name to debugger-8xk2p.
If you don't see a command prompt, try pressing enter.
/ # ps
PID   USER     COMMAND
    1 app      /app/checkout --port=8080
   27 root     sh
/ # wget -qO- localhost:8080/healthz
ok

Creating debugging pod node-debugger-node-b-q7h5m with container debugger on node node-b.
/ # chroot /host
sections.note: Ephemeral containers cannot be removed or restarted; they disappear when the pod does. Node debugging needs permission to create privileged pods, so restrict it with RBAC.

Likely cause

sections.title: About this example: checking node and control-plane health
sections.body: This session answers 'is the problem the workload or the platform?'. `kubectl get nodes` shows the Ready state, `describe node` shows the Conditions table (look for `MemoryPressure`, `DiskPressure`, `Ready`), and `/readyz?verbose` lists each API server health check. On managed clusters you cannot reach etcd or the control-plane hosts, so these API queries and your provider's status page are the main tools.

sections.title: Node conditions and API server readiness
sections.code:
kubectl get nodes
kubectl describe node node-c | sed -n '/Conditions:/,/Addresses:/p'
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose' | head -8
sections.output:

node-b   Ready      <none>          41d   v1.31.2
node-c   NotReady   <none>          41d   v1.31.2

sections.note: A node that stops posting status turns NotReady after node-monitor-grace-period (40s), and its pods are evicted after the taint toleration of 300s by default.

sections.title: etcd is the cluster's memory
sections.body: Back up etcd regularly (`etcdctl snapshot save`) and practice the restore. etcd needs fast disks (latency under 10 ms fsync) and an odd number of members; its default 2 GiB backend quota raises an alarm when full, after which the cluster becomes read-only until compaction and defrag.

sections.title: About this example: a postmortem template
sections.body: A postmortem is a blameless written record of an incident that produces concrete follow-up work. This file is a plain-text template (language `text`); copy it into your wiki for each incident of severity 2 or higher, and fill it within a few days while memory is fresh. Fields to focus on: the impact measured with the SLI, the timeline with timestamps, contributing factors (plural, never 'human error') and action items with owners and due dates.

sections.title: postmortem.md template
sections.code:
# Postmortem: <short title>   Severity: SEV2   Date: 2026-11-13

## Summary
One paragraph: what broke, for whom, for how long.

## Impact
- 31 minutes of elevated 5xx on checkout (peak 18%)
- Error budget consumed: 62% of the monthly budget

## Timeline (UTC)
09:02  Alert CheckoutErrorBudgetBurnFast fires
09:06  On-call acknowledges, declares SEV2
09:14  Cause suspected: new release 4.12
09:19  Rollback started (kubectl rollout undo)
09:33  Error ratio back under SLO

## Root cause and contributing factors
- ...

## What went well / what went badly / where we got lucky
- ...

## Action items
| Action | Owner | Due | Ticket |
|--------|-------|-----|--------|
| Add canary stage to the pipeline | alice | 2026-11-27 | OPS-412 |
sections.note: Blameless means asking how the system allowed the mistake, not who made it.

questions.question: Why use an ephemeral container?
options: To debug a pod whose image has no shell without restarting it
questions.explain: It adds a temporary container with tools to a running pod.

questions.question: What is the first priority in an incident?
questions.explain: Restore service first; investigate after the impact has stopped.

questions.question: Which condition indicates a node is short on disk?
questions.explain: DiskPressure True triggers eviction of pods.

questions.question: A good postmortem is...
options: Blameless with action items and owners
questions.explain: The goal is learning and concrete follow-ups.
